title: Unresponsive pitch, soft ball made it difficult for bowlers, says Gill
excerpt: The Indian captain also defended Mohammed Siraj's exclusion, stating that the tourists picked their best bowling combination for the game
author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Shubman Gill admitted that India were frustrated at not being able to force a result in Wellington, but felt there was nothing more they could have done on a surface that offered very little assistance to the bowlers through the first Test. New Zealand batted out 120 overs in their second innings to secure a draw, with Gill pointing to the flattening pitch and the ball losing its hardness early as major factors that made it difficult for India to take 20 wickets.

"Yes, I do feel a little frustrated. I didn't get the result that I wanted. But this is also a part of the game. We haven't drawn that many matches in the last six or seven years," Gill said at the post-match press conference.

India had New Zealand under pressure at 70 for 5 in the first innings before Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips staged a remarkable recovery, with the hosts posting 368. The visitors responded with 720 for 9 declared, but could not make regular inroads in the second innings as the home side batted through the final day, finishing at 239 for 5.
Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell blunted the Indian attack with an unbroken 63-run stand, as their marathon sixth-wicket stand lasted 43 overs before the players shook hands for the draw.
Gill felt the surface had become progressively flatter, leaving the bowlers very little to work with.

"When we started playing the Test match, we thought there would be a lot more in the wicket. Days three, four and five just got flatter and flatter. There was no impact of the overs being bowled on the wicket, or even the days being played. The wicket just got slower. Having seen that, I think it wasn't a great Test wicket, especially if you want results," he said.

Gill also pointed to the condition of the ball, revealing that it had become soft within 25-30 overs, making it difficult for the bowlers to generate enough movement or carry off the surface. He also questioned why the use of saliva, which was prohibited during the COVID-19 pandemic, continued to be disallowed.

"If the wicket doesn't help and the ball also becomes soft, it becomes very difficult for the bowlers to take wickets. They don't carry the edges. If there isn't much movement in the pitch, it becomes difficult to get batters out through LBWs as well. The ball definitely plays a big role," he said.

"We saw this in England as well. In the first three or four matches, the ball became soft very quickly. After 50 overs, the ball obviously will go soft, but if it is happening after 25-30 overs, it makes the job of the bowlers very difficult.

"I don't understand one thing: it's been so long since COVID, why hasn't the ball been allowed to be shined with saliva yet? We are way past COVID times. I do believe teams should be allowed to use saliva," added Gill.

The Indian captain also defended the decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI, describing it as a difficult call. Gill, however, maintained that the team had picked the best bowling attack for the conditions and backed the need to make selection decisions based on form.

"Siraj is a great player and a great bowler who has done very well for India. Before all of that, he's a really good friend of mine. We made our debuts together; even before playing for India, we were really good friends. Leaving him behind was a very tough decision for me as well," Gill said.

"But sometimes you have to see which bowlers are in form and which bowlers are bowling the best. I had this conversation with him and told him before the match that he was going to miss out. I don't know if he agreed or not, but he understood the logic behind it and why we picked someone else ahead of him. He's one of those characters who always wants to come back and do well for the team."

Asked whether India would consider changes to their combination for the next game, Gill indicated that the team was unlikely to make wholesale changes, although the nature of the pitch would remain a key consideration.

"Honestly, not really. Maybe we'll see how the wicket is, but I think most of the team is going to be the same. I thought everyone did decently well. All our bowlers did well. I don't think the batting would have done anything more. Most of the team would almost be similar, but again, we'll go there and see how the wicket is. This wicket didn't play out how we thought it was going to, so we'll see once we get there."
